parts.context: Two university students who share a rented house are discussing a message from their landlord.

lines: Callum, have you checked your email? Mr. Dhaliwal sent us both something this morning.
I saw it, but I only read the first line. Something about the house being listed?

He’s selling it. The real estate agent wants to start showings next week, and he says the buyers will probably want it empty. He’s offering us a thousand dollars each if we’re out by the end of February.
The end of February? That’s right in the middle of midterms. I’ve got three exams that week alone.
I know. And the thing is, our lease doesn’t end until April thirtieth. I’m not sure he can just ask us to leave.
Well, technically he’s asking, not ordering. A thousand dollars each is tempting, though. That’s almost a month’s rent.

It’s tempting until you realize that every other place near campus costs at least three hundred more than we pay here. We’d burn through that money in about three months, and then we’d be paying more for the rest of the year.
Fair. And moving in the middle of winter isn’t exactly fun either. What about the showings? Does he say how often?
Up to four a week, with twenty-four hours’ notice. He says we don’t have to be home for them.
Four a week? I study at the kitchen table. I can’t have strangers wandering through the place while I’m in the middle of practice problems.
Neither can I, honestly. Okay, before we answer him, let’s figure out what our options really are.

qs.q: Why did Mr. Dhaliwal contact the roommates?
o: To tell them their lease will not be renewed in April
To offer them money to move out before their lease ends
To inform them that the rent will increase after the sale
To ask them to show the house to potential buyers
qs.ev: He’s offering us a thousand dollars each if we’re out by the end of February
qs.x: He offers a payment if they leave by February, before the lease ends in April. The agent, not the students, will hold the showings, and no rent increase is mentioned.

qs.q: Why does Ji-woo think the offer is less attractive than it first appears?
o: The payment would have to be shared between the two of them.
They would lose their damage deposit if they moved out early.
Higher rents elsewhere would soon use up the money.
Moving companies charge much more during the winter.
qs.ev: every other place near campus costs at least three hundred more than we pay here
qs.x: Rent elsewhere is at least $300 more, so the payment would be gone in about three months. The offer is a thousand dollars each, not a shared amount.

qs.q: What is Callum’s main concern about the showings?
o: They would disturb the space where he studies.
Strangers might take some of his belongings.
He would have to be at home for every visit.
The landlord would not give them enough notice.
qs.ev: I study at the kitchen table
qs.x: He studies at the kitchen table and cannot work with strangers walking through. Ji-woo says they do not have to be home, and 24 hours’ notice will be given.

lines: Okay, option one: residence. My cousin said spaces sometimes open up in January when people drop out.

I actually called the housing office yesterday, just in case. They have a few rooms in Thornbury Hall, but they’re singles at eleven fifty a month, and you have to buy the meal plan on top of that. For both of us, that’s way over budget.
Okay, scratch that. What about Nadia’s place? She’s going on exchange to Lyon in March and wants someone to sublet.
Her apartment’s nice, but it’s out past the airport. It’s a ninety-minute bus ride each way, and the night bus stops running at eleven. You have lab until ten on Thursdays.
Yeah, I’d basically be living on the bus. So the other option is that we just stay. I mean, if the lease runs until April, can he actually make us leave?

That’s what I want to find out. I read online that selling a house doesn’t end a lease, but if the buyer wants to move in personally, the rules might be different. I don’t trust what I read on a random forum, though.
The student union has a legal clinic, doesn’t it? It’s free for students.
It does, but they only take appointments on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and they book up fast.
Then that’s our first step. I’d rather know our rights before we say yes or no to anything.

qs.q: Why do they reject the residence option?
o: No rooms there will become available until the fall term.
Thornbury Hall does not offer students a meal plan option.
Only first-year students are allowed to apply for rooms.
It would cost far more than they can afford.
qs.ev: For both of us, that’s way over budget
qs.x: Rooms are available, but singles at $1,150 plus a meal plan are “way over budget”. The meal plan is required, not missing.

qs.q: What is the main problem with Nadia’s apartment?
o: Nadia wants them to pay rent for the whole year.
Its location makes getting to campus very inconvenient.
The building does not allow two people to sublet.
It is much more expensive than their current house.
qs.ev: It’s a ninety-minute bus ride each way
qs.x: The apartment is ninety minutes away by bus and the night bus stops at eleven. Cost and sublet rules are never raised as problems.

qs.q: What does Ji-woo suggest about the information she found online?
o: She is confident it proves they can stay until April.
She believes the buyer will definitely want to move in.
She is not sure it can be relied on.
She found it on the student union’s website.
qs.ev: I don’t trust what I read on a random forum
qs.x: She does not trust a “random forum”, so she doubts the information. She mentions the buyer moving in only as a possibility.

lines: Okay, I just checked the clinic’s booking page. There’s a slot next Tuesday at two.
I’ve got a tutorial at two. Could you go without me?
I could, but I’d rather you came. They’ll want to see the lease, and it’s in your name as well as mine.
Then I’ll skip the tutorial. It’s only review, and Professor Lam posts the slides anyway. What do we tell Mr. Dhaliwal in the meantime?
Nothing that commits us. Just thank him and say we’re looking into our options and will get back to him by the end of next week.
And the showings? Should we push back on four a week?
I think we can ask, politely, whether he’d limit them to weekends. He’s always been decent to us. Remember when the furnace died in January and he had someone here within an hour?
True. I don’t want to burn that bridge. And honestly, if the clinic says we can stay until April, I’d be fine moving in May. Everyone leaves then anyway, so there’ll be loads of places.
Exactly, and we wouldn’t be packing boxes during exams. Okay, I’ll draft the email to him tonight and send it to you before it goes out.
Sounds good. And let’s not mention the clinic in the email. I don’t want him to think we’re getting ready for a fight.

qs.q: Why does Callum decide to miss his tutorial?
o: Ji-woo refuses to go to the appointment on her own.
The clinic needs both tenants to sign a legal form.
His name also appears on the document the clinic will check.
His professor has cancelled the tutorial this week.
qs.ev: it’s in your name as well as mine
qs.x: The clinic will want the lease, which is in both names, so his presence matters. Ji-woo says she could go alone, and the tutorial is not cancelled; it is only review.

qs.q: How does Ji-woo feel about the landlord?
o: She thinks he has generally treated them fairly.
She suspects he is trying to trick them into leaving.
She feels he is too slow to respond to repairs.
She believes he will refuse any request they make.
qs.ev: He’s always been decent to us
qs.x: She calls him “decent” and recalls a fast furnace repair, the opposite of option C. Nothing suggests she thinks he is tricking them.

parts.context: A father is meeting with the director of his son’s child care centre.

lines: Thanks for calling me in, Ms. Abernathy. I have to admit, when I saw the note in Felix’s cubby, my stomach dropped. Is he in trouble?

Not in trouble, no. I wanted to talk in person because notes can sound more alarming than they’re meant to. Felix bit another child on Monday and again yesterday. The second time, it broke the skin, so we had to fill out an incident report.
Oh no. Is the other child okay? Should I contact the parents to apologize?
The child is fine, and I appreciate the thought, but we don’t share families’ names. Our privacy policy is quite strict on that. I’ve passed on that you were concerned, though.
I understand. I just feel awful. He’s never done anything like this at home.

Biting at twenty-two months is far more common than parents think. Children that age have big feelings and very few words, and biting gets a reaction fast. What we’ve noticed is that both incidents happened just before lunch, when the group is moving from outdoor play to the tables. That’s when he’s tired and there’s a lot of noise.
Before lunch. That might make sense, actually. We have a new baby at home, and since she arrived, Felix has been waking up at five most mornings.

That’s really helpful to know. Here’s what we’d like to do. For the next two weeks, one of our educators, Jasmine, will stay close to him during transitions. If she sees him getting frustrated, she’ll redirect him before it escalates. We’ll also use the same short phrase every time, “Gentle teeth, we bite food,” and it would help if you said the same thing at home.
Of course. Is there a point where he’d be asked to leave the centre? I’ve heard stories.

I know the stories you mean. Our policy is that if there are three incidents in a month, we hold a formal meeting and write a behaviour plan together. Removing a child is a last resort, and honestly, in eleven years, I’ve never seen biting get that far.
That’s a relief. Could I come in a bit earlier at pickup on Friday to see how it’s going?
Absolutely. Jasmine finishes at four, so try to come before then.

qs.q: Why did the director ask to meet the father in person?
o: Felix had to be sent home early that day.
The other child’s parents had made a complaint.
She needed him to sign the incident report.
She did not want a written message to worry him.
qs.ev: notes can sound more alarming than they’re meant to
qs.x: She explains that notes can sound more alarming than intended. An incident report was filled out, but she never says he must sign it, and no complaint is mentioned.

qs.q: Why can the father not contact the other family?
o: The centre does not reveal who other families are.
The other parents are still very upset about it.
The other child’s injury was too minor to matter.
The director has already apologized on his behalf.
qs.ev: we don’t share families’ names
qs.x: The privacy policy prevents sharing names. She passes on his concern but does not apologize for him, and the injury did break the skin.

qs.q: According to the director, when has Felix been biting?
o: During outdoor play when other children take his toys
At pickup time, when he sees his father arrive
During the noisy, tiring period before a meal
First thing in the morning when he is dropped off
qs.ev: both incidents happened just before lunch
qs.x: Both incidents happened just before lunch, during a loud transition when he is tired. Outdoor play is what comes before that transition, not when the biting occurred.

qs.q: What does the father’s comment about the new baby suggest?
o: Felix has also been biting his sister at home.
Felix’s behaviour may be linked to tiredness and family change.
The family is thinking of moving Felix to another centre.
Felix no longer takes an afternoon nap at the centre.
qs.ev: Felix has been waking up at five most mornings
qs.x: Since the baby arrived, Felix wakes at five, which connects to the director’s point that he bites when tired. The father says he has never bitten at home.

qs.q: What does the director imply about the chance of Felix being asked to leave?
o: It will happen automatically after a third incident.
It depends mainly on how the other family reacts.
It becomes likely if the two-week plan does not work.
It is extremely unlikely to happen in his case.
qs.ev: in eleven years, I’ve never seen biting get that far
qs.x: She has never seen biting lead to removal in eleven years, so it is very unlikely. Three incidents lead to a meeting and a plan, not automatic removal.

parts.context: A parent calls the city recreation department about March break day camps.

lines: Hi, I’m calling about the March break day camps. I’d like to register my two kids, but I have some questions first.
Happy to help. How old are the children?
Owen is nine, and Tilly is five. She turns six on March twenty-second.

Okay. Adventure Camp is for ages six to twelve, and children have to be six by the first day of camp, which is March sixteenth. So Owen is fine, but unfortunately Tilly wouldn’t be eligible this year, even though she’s only a week off.
Oh, that’s a shame. She’ll be crushed. Is there anything for her?
There’s Little Explorers, for four- and five-year-olds. It’s mornings only, nine to noon, in the same building, so drop-off would be easy. It’s a hundred and ten dollars for the week.
Mornings only. I work until four thirty, so that doesn’t really solve my problem, but I’ll think about it. What does Owen’s camp cost?

Adventure Camp is a hundred and ninety-five for the week, which covers nine to four. If you need us before nine or after four, extended care is an extra thirty-five for the week, and it runs from seven thirty to five thirty.
I’ll definitely need that. Now, we only moved here in January. Do I pay the resident rate?
If you live within city limits, yes, but you’ll need proof of address when you register.
My driver’s licence still has our old address. Would our lease work? We signed it in December.
Unfortunately, we don’t accept leases, because they don’t confirm you’re actually living there. A recent hydro or internet bill would be the easiest.
Okay, I can do that. What about field trips?

On Wednesday, the group goes to the Science Discovery Centre. You’ll need to sign a permission form and pay twelve dollars for admission. Otherwise, kids bring a nut-free lunch and two snacks every day.

February third at seven p.m. for residents. My advice is to set up your account and add both children before the third. Every year, people lose their spot because they’re creating a password while the popular weeks fill up.
Good tip. And if something comes up and I need to cancel?

You’ll get a full refund, minus a ten-dollar admin fee, up to seven days before camp starts. After that, we can only offer a credit toward another program, unless there’s a medical reason with a doctor’s note.

qs.q: Why is Tilly not eligible for Adventure Camp?
o: She will not have reached the minimum age when it starts.
Little Explorers is reserved for children who are five.
The camp is already full for children under seven.
She would need extended care, which is not offered.
qs.ev: children have to be six by the first day of camp
qs.x: Tilly turns six on March 22, after camp begins on March 16. Extended care is offered, and nothing says the camp is full.

qs.q: How much will Colleen pay for Owen’s week, including the care she needs?
qs.ev: extended care is an extra thirty-five for the week
qs.x: She works until 4:30, so Owen needs extended care: $195 + $35 = $230. The $12 trip fee is a separate admission charge, not part of the camp fee.

qs.q: What can Colleen use to prove that she lives in the city?
o: Her driver’s licence, once she updates the old address
A recent bill for a service at her home
The lease she and her family signed in December
A letter from the children’s new school
qs.ev: A recent hydro or internet bill would be the easiest
qs.x: A recent hydro or internet bill is accepted. Leases are specifically not accepted because they do not prove someone lives there.

qs.q: What is needed for the Wednesday outing?
o: Money for the gift shop at the science centre
A parent to drive their own child there
A signed form and a small additional fee
A nut-free lunch in a separate labelled bag
qs.ev: You’ll need to sign a permission form and pay twelve dollars for admission
qs.x: The trip requires a permission form and twelve dollars. A nut-free lunch is required every day, not specifically for the trip.

qs.q: What does the agent advise Colleen to do?
o: Prepare her online account before registration opens
Register Owen first and add Tilly later in the week
Phone the office at seven p.m. on February third
Choose a less popular week to be sure of a space
qs.ev: set up your account and add both children before the third
qs.x: He recommends setting up the account in advance so she does not lose time on the night. Seven p.m. is when online registration opens, not a time to phone.

qs.q: If Colleen cancels four days before camp starts, with no medical reason, what will happen?
o: She will receive a full refund.
She will be refunded all but ten dollars.
She will lose all the money she paid.
She will receive credit toward another program.
qs.ev: After that, we can only offer a credit toward another program
qs.x: The refund minus $10 applies only up to seven days before; four days is too late, so she gets a credit. She does not lose the money entirely.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a change to kindergarten classes.

lines: Starting next September, no kindergarten class in the province will be allowed to have more than twenty-two students. The education minister made the announcement this morning, calling it the most significant change to early learning in a decade. Currently, kindergarten classes average about twenty-six children, and the legal maximum is twenty-nine. The province is committing ninety million dollars over two years to hire additional teachers and early childhood educators. But school boards say the plan has a glaring gap. Not a cent of the money is for space, and in fast-growing suburbs, many schools are already full. Deepa Raman chairs the Eastgate District School Board.

Let me be clear: we support smaller classes. The research on young children is strong. But you can’t split one class of twenty-eight into two classes without a second room. Our board alone estimates we’ll need thirty-five new portables, at roughly two hundred and fifty thousand dollars each once you include installation and washrooms. A cap without classrooms is a promise on paper.

The ministry says boards that can show they have no available space may apply for a one-year exemption, but their plans must be submitted by March first. Staffing is another concern. Each kindergarten class is led by a teacher working alongside an early childhood educator, and colleges report that enrolment in early childhood education programs has dropped by nearly a fifth over the past five years, as graduates choose better-paid jobs in other fields. Parent groups have largely welcomed the announcement, but some are uneasy about one possible side effect. To meet the cap in crowded neighbourhoods, some children could be redirected to schools outside their neighbourhood, at least temporarily. The minister said that would be a last resort, and she promised that families would be consulted before any child was moved. Boards are expected to publish their space plans by the end of the school year.

qs.q: What will change next September?
o: The average kindergarten class will fall to twenty-six.
Every kindergarten class will receive a second teacher.
No kindergarten class may exceed twenty-two children.
Kindergarten will become a full-day program everywhere.
qs.ev: no kindergarten class in the province will be allowed to have more than twenty-two students
qs.x: The new rule sets a maximum of twenty-two. Twenty-six is the current average, not the new target.

qs.q: What is the school boards’ main criticism of the plan?
o: It provides no funding for extra classrooms.
It does not hire enough early childhood educators.
It was announced without consulting parent groups.
It will lower the quality of kindergarten teaching.
qs.ev: Not a cent of the money is for space
qs.x: The “glaring gap” is that none of the money pays for space. The educator shortage is a separate concern raised later in the report.

qs.q: What does Ms. Raman mean by “a promise on paper”?
o: The government has broken similar promises before.
The new limit will have to be written into law.
Parents will need to sign new enrolment forms.
The rule may be impossible to carry out in reality.
qs.ev: A cap without classrooms is a promise on paper
qs.x: Without rooms, the limit exists only in writing and cannot be achieved in practice. She says nothing about past broken promises or legislation.

qs.q: What must a board do to delay the new rule?
o: Hire more early childhood educators before March
Prove it lacks space and submit a plan on time
Install portables before the school year begins
Obtain approval from local parent groups first
qs.ev: boards that can show they have no available space may apply for a one-year exemption
qs.x: An exemption requires showing there is no space and submitting plans by March 1. Installing portables is what boards want to do, not a condition for delay.

qs.q: What worries some parent groups?
o: Class sizes may increase in other grades.
Teachers may leave for better-paid jobs.
Some children may not attend their local school.
Portables may be uncomfortable in winter.
qs.ev: some children could be redirected to schools outside their neighbourhood
qs.x: Parents fear children may be sent to schools outside their neighbourhood. Better-paid jobs elsewhere relate to educator graduates, not teachers or parents’ concerns.

parts.context: Two parents and their sixteen-year-old daughter are discussing her plans for the summer.

lines: Zara, your dad and I wanted to talk about the summer before the deadlines start piling up. Did you look at the brochure I left on your desk?
The biology program at Northbrook University? I looked at it. It’s four weeks, and it’s twenty-four hundred dollars. That’s a lot of money to spend on going to school in the summer.
It’s an investment. You’d be working in a real lab, and the professors write reference letters for students who do well. That could make a real difference when you apply to university next year.

Or I could take the job at Greenleaf Garden Centre. Mrs. Pham already said she’d hire me full-time for July and August at sixteen fifty an hour. By September I’d have almost four thousand dollars saved.
I have to say, I’m with Zara on this one, Lorraine. When I was her age, my first job taught me more about responsibility than any classroom did. And she’d be earning money instead of spending it.
Desmond, nobody’s saying a job isn’t valuable. But she can work for the rest of her life. How often does a sixteen-year-old get to do research at a university?
Mom, I’m not even sure I want to do biology. Last year I wanted to be a vet, and now I’m thinking about environmental engineering.
That’s exactly why the program would help. You’d find out whether you actually enjoy lab work before you commit four years to it.
Hmm. That’s actually a fair point. I hadn’t thought of it as a way to test the waters.
Dad! You were on my side two minutes ago.
I’m on the side of whatever makes sense. But the money is a big issue. Is it twenty-four hundred plus a residence fee?
No, residence is included. And there’s something I didn’t mention. They offer bursaries. Students with an average over eighty-five can apply for one that covers half.
So we’d be looking at twelve hundred. That changes the picture.
Okay, but if I’m away in July, Mrs. Pham might give the job to someone else. She needs people for the whole summer.
It says August fourth to the twenty-ninth.
Then what about this? Ask Mrs. Pham if you could start in May, on weekends, and work full-time through July. You’d still earn a decent amount, maybe two-thirds of what you planned.
I suppose I could ask her. She did say weekends are her busiest time in the spring, with everyone buying plants.

Then I’ll look for something else. There are other jobs. Honestly, if the bursary comes through, I’d like to try the program. It’s the essay I’m worried about. The application wants five hundred words on a scientific question that interests me.
You could write about the wetland project you did in Grade Ten. You talked about it for weeks.
That’s actually not a bad idea.
So here’s the plan. Zara talks to Mrs. Pham this weekend and starts the application tonight. When’s the deadline?
March fifteenth for the bursary, April first for the program itself.
Then the bursary deadline is the one that matters. Let’s aim to have a draft of the essay by next Sunday.
Fine. But if I get in, I’m still keeping some of my garden centre money for a car.

qs.q: Why does Lorraine favour the biology program?
o: It is the least expensive of the options available.
It could strengthen Zara’s future university applications.
It would let Zara earn credits toward her degree.
It is taught by a professor whom Lorraine knows.
qs.ev: That could make a real difference when you apply to university next year
qs.x: Lab work and reference letters could help Zara’s university applications. Nothing is said about earning credits, and it costs money while the job earns it.

qs.q: Why does Desmond first support Zara’s plan to work?
o: He thinks the program would be too difficult for her.
He wants her to start paying for her own car.
He doubts that Zara is truly interested in biology.
He believes a job helps young people grow up.
qs.ev: my first job taught me more about responsibility than any classroom did
qs.x: He says his first job taught him responsibility, so he values work for building maturity. The car is Zara’s idea at the end, and her doubt about biology comes from her, not him.

qs.q: What makes Desmond change his mind?
o: The idea that the program could help Zara explore a career
The news that the program includes a free residence room
Zara’s admission that she wants to become a veterinarian
Lorraine’s claim that Zara can work for the rest of her life
qs.ev: I hadn’t thought of it as a way to test the waters
qs.x: He changes after hearing the program could show whether Zara enjoys lab work, “a way to test the waters”. Residence comes up later, and the vet plan was last year’s idea.

qs.q: How does Zara react when her father changes his position?
o: She is relieved that her parents finally agree.
She refuses to discuss the program any further.
She is surprised and feels he has let her down.
She assumes he is only joking with her mother.
qs.ev: Dad! You were on my side two minutes ago.
qs.x: Her exclamation shows surprise and a sense of being abandoned. She keeps discussing the plan afterward, so she does not refuse to talk.

qs.q: How much would the program cost the family if Zara receives the bursary?
o: $1,200 plus residence
qs.ev: So we’d be looking at twelve hundred.
qs.x: The bursary covers half of $2,400, leaving $1,200, and residence is already included. Option C ignores that residence costs nothing extra.

qs.q: What does Desmond suggest about the garden centre job?
o: Zara should work full-time only during August.
Zara should turn the job down for this year.
Zara should ask Mrs. Pham for a higher wage.
Zara should change her hours so she can do both.
qs.ev: Ask Mrs. Pham if you could start in May, on weekends, and work full-time through July
qs.x: He proposes starting earlier on weekends and working full-time through July, leaving August free for the program. August is when she would be away, so option A is the reverse.

qs.q: What does Zara mean when she says, “That’s actually not a bad idea”?
o: She is pleasantly surprised by her mother’s suggestion.
She still prefers to choose a different essay topic.
She thinks her mother is trying to write the essay.
She has already started writing about the project.
qs.ev: That’s actually not a bad idea.
qs.x: “Actually not a bad idea” is mild, slightly surprised approval of the wetland topic. She has been worried about the essay, so she has not started it yet.

qs.q: Which deadline will the family focus on first?
o: April first, for the program application
Next Sunday, for the final application
March fifteenth, for the financial award
This weekend, for the job decision
qs.ev: Then the bursary deadline is the one that matters
qs.x: Lorraine says the bursary deadline, March 15, matters most. Next Sunday is for a draft, not the final application, and April 1 is the later program deadline.

parts.context: You will hear a report about online portals that let parents see their children’s marks.

lines: For most of the last century, parents learned how their children were doing at school a few times a year, when report cards came home. Today, many families can check a mark within hours of a test being graded. Online parent portals, now used by most school boards in the country, were introduced with a simple promise: no more surprises in June. Many parents say the portals have delivered exactly that. A mother of three in Regina told us she caught her son’s slide in math in October, not at the end of the term, and arranged tutoring in time to turn things around. Parents who share custody across two households also say the portals put both of them on equal footing, so neither depends on the other to pass along information. But a growing number of teachers argue that the constant flow of data has a cost. They describe students who check the app between classes, parents who email about a single quiz before the student has even seen the mark, and teenagers who no longer feel the work is theirs. Some boards have responded with a delay: marks appear for students forty-eight hours before parents can see them, giving young people the chance to break the news themselves. Dr. Ruairi Doyle, a psychologist who works with adolescents, says the tool itself is not the problem.

Access to information is not harmful. What matters is what parents do with it. If a parent sees a sixty-two and the first thing the child hears is “What happened?”, the portal becomes a surveillance device. If the parent waits and asks, “How did that test feel?”, it can actually open a conversation. I’d be wary of any policy that treats the technology as the villain. The habits we bring to it are what count.

Not everyone finds that persuasive. Some teachers say the forty-eight-hour delay is too short to make a real difference and would prefer marks to be released weekly, in batches. Others worry that a weekly release would bring back exactly the surprises the portals were meant to prevent. Students themselves, when asked, were surprisingly split. In one survey of high school students in Manitoba, just over half said they would turn off parent notifications if they could, but a third said the portal helped them stay organized and keep track of missing work. For now, most boards are leaving the decision to individual schools, which means that two students in the same city may have very different experiences. Several boards say they will survey families again next spring before deciding whether to set a single policy for all of their schools.

qs.q: According to the report, what was the original goal of parent portals?
o: To make sure parents were not caught off guard by results
To reduce the number of report cards sent home each year
To let teachers communicate with students more quickly
To help separated parents organize custody schedules
qs.ev: no more surprises in June
qs.x: The promise was “no more surprises in June”, meaning parents would not be shocked by end-of-year results. Separated parents benefit, but custody schedules were not the purpose.

qs.q: Why do some parents who share custody value the portals?
o: They reduce the need for parent-teacher interviews.
They let parents see marks before their children do.
Each parent gets the same information directly.
They allow parents to book tutoring online.
qs.ev: the portals put both of them on equal footing
qs.x: Both parents see the same information, so neither depends on the other. Seeing marks before children is the situation some boards are trying to prevent.

p1.meta: From: Yolanda Brisebois  |  To: Inès Tremblay  |  Subject: Back to school at 44!
p1.text:
Hi Inès,

Sorry I’ve been so quiet lately. I finally did it: I enrolled in the part-time bookkeeping certificate at Lakeshore College! Classes started three weeks ago, and I’m already wondering how I ever thought I’d have free time.

The program runs Tuesday and Thursday evenings from 6:30 to 9:30, and there’s a group project every term. My group is great, although at forty-four I’m old enough to be the mother of two of them. They’re lightning-fast with spreadsheets, but they had never seen an actual invoice until I brought some in from the office. I think we’re learning from each other.

I was terrified about the first test. I hadn’t written an exam in over twenty years, and I spent the whole weekend before it convinced I’d fail. I got an 82. I may have cried a little in the parking lot.

Now for the reason I’m writing. As you know, Andrés started a new job in September that has him on the road most of the week. Until now, my mother has been watching Benji and Rosa on class nights, but she’s just started physiotherapy for her hip, and her appointments are on Tuesday evenings for the next ten weeks. Thursdays are fine, since Andrés is always home by then.

Would there be any chance you could come over on Tuesdays, from about 5:45 until I get home around 10? The kids will have eaten, and they’re usually asleep by 8:30, so it would mostly be sitting on my couch watching your shows. I would of course pay you, or, if you’d rather, I could take your girls for a weekend so you and Kwame can finally go away.

If it’s too much, please say so. I’ve also looked into a babysitter from the college’s student job board, but I’d feel much better leaving them with someone they know.

Either way, thank you for always cheering me on. When I told you last spring that I was thinking of going back to school, you were the only person who didn’t ask, “At your age?”

Big hugs,
Yolanda

p3.title: Under One Roof: The Return of the Multigenerational Home
paras: When the most recent census results were released, one figure caught many observers by surprise: households in which three or more generations live together were the fastest-growing type of household in the country. Although such homes still represent a small share of the total, their number grew at roughly twice the rate of all households over the previous decade. Housing costs explain part of the trend. In cities where a modest detached house now sells for well over a million dollars, pooling incomes is often the only way for younger families to buy. But economics is not the whole story. For many immigrant families, living with grandparents is simply the norm, and newcomers have settled in large numbers in the very suburbs where multigenerational homes are most common.

Families who live this way often describe benefits that are hard to put a price on. Grandparents who are home during the day can provide child care, saving parents thousands of dollars a year and sparing children long days in daycare. In return, older relatives can remain in a family setting rather than moving to a retirement residence, and help is close at hand if their health declines. Some researchers also point to subtler advantages. Children raised alongside grandparents are more likely to speak a heritage language fluently, according to one study of families in two provinces, and grandparents report feeling less isolated. “My mother used to call me three times a day because she was lonely,” one Calgary father said. “Now she’s too busy with the kids to call anyone.”

None of this means that sharing a home is easy. The most common complaint is a lack of privacy, particularly in houses that were never designed for two or three households. Disagreements over child-rearing are another source of tension; a grandmother who believes children should finish everything on their plate may clash with parents who were taught not to force a child to eat. Family therapists say the most successful arrangements are those in which expectations are discussed openly before anyone moves in, including who pays for what, who does the cooking, and what happens if the arrangement no longer works. Families who skip that conversation, they warn, often find that small irritations, such as noise late at night or a borrowed car returned with an empty tank, build into lasting resentment.

Governments and lenders are slowly adjusting. Several cities have changed their zoning rules to allow secondary suites and small backyard homes, sometimes called garden suites, which give older relatives a separate front door on the same property. A few banks now offer mortgages that take into account the income of every adult who will live in the home, not just the buyers named on the title. Builders, too, are taking notice: some new subdivisions advertise floor plans with a second kitchen and a main-floor bedroom with its own bathroom. Critics point out, however, that zoning changes have done little in older neighbourhoods, where lots are narrow, permits can take many months and renovation costs remain high.

p4.title: An A Should Mean Something Again
p4.byline: Opinion | by Reginald Thiessen, former university admissions director
p4.text:
When I began reading university applications in the late 1990s, an average above ninety percent was rare enough to make me sit up. By the time I retired last year, it was routine. At some high schools, more than a third of graduating students now apply with averages in the nineties. Either Canadian teenagers have become dramatically smarter in a single generation, or something has happened to our grades. I suspect the latter.

Grade inflation is not a conspiracy. It is the result of many small, understandable pressures. Teachers face parents who argue over every mark, knowing that a single percentage point can decide a scholarship. Schools compete for students and like to advertise strong results. And when the school down the road is generous, no principal wants her students to be the ones penalized for honest marking. Each decision makes sense on its own; together, they have hollowed out the meaning of an A.

The people who pay the price are students themselves. When nearly everyone has a ninety, universities lose the ability to tell applicants apart, and admission becomes partly a lottery. Worse, students arrive believing they have mastered material they have not. Every September, first-year instructors see students with excellent high school marks struggle with basic algebra or essay structure, and every November, some of those students conclude, wrongly, that they do not belong at university at all. A high mark that does not reflect real skill is not a gift. It is a debt that comes due later.

There is also a fairness problem. Because inflation varies from school to school, a ninety from one school may be worth an eighty-two from another. Admissions officers know this, and some quietly adjust for it, relying on their impressions of particular schools. That practice tends to favour applicants from well-known schools and to disadvantage students from small towns or newer schools whose reputations are not yet established.

What should be done? I propose that every province introduce a common examination in a small number of core Grade 12 subjects, worth thirty percent of the final mark. Some provinces have done this in the past and abandoned it; I believe they gave up too soon. A shared exam would not replace teachers’ judgment. Seventy percent of the mark would still come from classroom work, which captures skills, such as research, collaboration and persistence, that no exam can measure. But the exam would act as an anchor, a common reference point that lets a ninety mean roughly the same thing in a northern town as in a large city.

I am aware that many teachers and parents worry about exam stress, and I do not dismiss that concern. Some students who shine elsewhere freeze in a test hall. That is precisely why I would cap the exam at thirty percent, and why students should have a chance to rewrite it once. What I cannot accept is the idea that the alternative, a system in which marks steadily lose their meaning, is somehow kinder.

Universities have a role, too. They should publish, school by school, how their admitted students actually perform in first year. Such data would show families which high marks hold up and might encourage schools to mark honestly.

An A should be a signal, not a formality. Right now, it is drifting toward the latter.

To suggest that today’s students are less intelligent than before
To explain the reasons why he finally decided to retire
To argue that universities should admit fewer students
qs.ev: By the time I retired last year, it was routine.
qs.x: He contrasts how rare 90%+ averages were then with how routine they are now. He actually doubts students became smarter, but he never says they are less intelligent.

t1.situation: Yesterday, your three-year-old daughter came home from her child care centre with a large bruise on her forehead and a scratch on her cheek. No one mentioned it when you picked her up, and you did not receive an incident report.
bullets: Describe what you noticed and when
Say what you would like the centre to do
t1.model:
Dear Ms. Whitford,

I am writing about my daughter, Ayla, who is in the Bluebird room. When I picked her up yesterday at 5:15, she seemed unusually quiet, and when I took off her hat in the car, I noticed a large bruise on her forehead and a scratch on her left cheek. Nobody mentioned anything at pickup, and there was no incident report in her cubby.

I understand that toddlers fall and bump into things, and I am not assuming anyone did anything wrong. However, I am concerned that I had to discover the injury myself. Ayla told me another child pushed her near the slide, but at three, her account may not be reliable.

Could you please find out from the staff on duty how and when she was hurt, and send me a written incident report? I would also like to discuss how the centre makes sure parents are told about injuries, especially late in the day when educators change shifts.

Thank you for looking into this.

Sincerely,
Nathaniel Brooks

t2.intro: Your local community centre has received funding for one new free program and has asked residents to vote on how the money should be used.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: Free evening language classes in English and French for adult newcomers, two evenings a week, with child care provided during classes.
t2.b: A free after-school sports program for youth aged 10 to 15, three afternoons a week, including basketball, soccer and climbing, with trained coaches.
t2.model:
Both programs would benefit our neighbourhood, but I prefer Option A, the free evening language classes for adult newcomers.

The most important reason is that language is the key to almost everything else. Without strong English or French, newcomers struggle to find jobs that match their qualifications, to speak with their children’s teachers, or even to explain symptoms to a doctor. Many of them are engineers, nurses or accountants who end up in low-paid work simply because of language. Free classes could change the direction of an entire family’s life.

I also appreciate that child care is included. Parents, especially mothers, often skip classes because they have no one to watch their children in the evening. This feature makes the program genuinely accessible.

Of course, youth sports are valuable too. They keep teenagers active and out of trouble after school. However, our city already offers subsidized sports through school teams and community leagues, while free language classes in the evening are very hard to find.

For these reasons, I believe Option A would make the greatest difference.

t1.prompt: Your friend is thinking about taking her two children, aged eight and eleven, out of school to homeschool them. She works part-time from home. Advise your friend about what she should consider before making this decision.
t1.model: Wow, that’s a big decision, and I can see why you’re thinking about it, but I’d take a few months to plan before you pull them out. First, be really honest about your time. Working part-time from home sounds flexible, but teaching two kids at different grade levels is basically a full-time job. Try sketching out a typical day on paper, with your work hours and their lessons, and see if it actually fits. Second, find out what the rules are in our province. You’ll probably have to notify the school board, and there may be requirements about subjects or assessments. Third, think about the social side. At eight and eleven, their friendships really matter. If you go ahead, I’d sign them up for team sports or a homeschool co-op, so they’re still around other kids every week. I’d also talk to the kids themselves. Your eleven-year-old especially might have strong feelings, and they’ll cooperate much more if they feel involved. Finally, you don’t have to make it permanent. Maybe try it for one school year and then reassess. If it doesn’t work, they can always go back. Either way, I’m happy to help, and you know I’d take them to the science museum anytime.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you learned a new skill as an adult. What was the skill, and how did the experience go?
t2.model: About three years ago, when I turned thirty-five, I finally decided to learn how to swim properly. I’d always been embarrassed about it, because I grew up in a town without a public pool, so I could only splash around in the shallow end. I signed up for adult lessons at the community centre on Tuesday nights. The first class was honestly humiliating. Everyone else seemed to float effortlessly, and I swallowed so much water I was coughing for ten minutes. But my instructor, a retired lifeguard named Doreen, was incredibly patient. She broke everything down into tiny steps, like just putting my face in the water and breathing out. After about two months, I swam my first full length without stopping. Last summer, I swam across a small lake at my friend’s cottage. I felt so proud.

scene.alt: A busy family kitchen on a weekend afternoon. On the left, a grandmother with grey hair in a bun and a blue apron-coloured shirt stands at the counter holding a tray of cookies. A young girl in a pink shirt stands beside her holding a mixing bowl. In the centre, a grandfather with glasses sits at a wooden table with a small boy, and there is a birthday cake on the table. On the right, a mother in a green shirt is talking on her phone near the window, and a grey cat is sitting on the floor. There is a clock on the wall, a shelf and a plant.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This picture shows a family kitchen, and it looks like they’re getting ready for a birthday. On the left side, there’s a grandmother with grey hair in a bun, wearing a blue dress, and she’s standing at the counter holding a tray of freshly baked cookies. Next to her, a little girl in a pink shirt is holding a bowl, so she’s probably helping with the baking. In the middle of the room, there’s a wooden table with a birthday cake on it. A grandfather with glasses is sitting there, and a small boy in a yellow shirt is standing across from him, staring at the cake. On the right, a woman in a green shirt, maybe the mother, is talking on her phone by the window, and a grey cat is sitting on the floor near her feet. It feels warm and cheerful.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the mother on the phone is probably talking to someone who’s coming to the party, maybe giving them directions, and soon the doorbell will ring and more relatives will arrive. Meanwhile, the little boy can’t take his eyes off the cake, so I bet he’ll try to sneak a taste of the icing with his finger when he thinks nobody is looking. The grandfather will probably notice and laugh, and maybe pretend not to see. The grandmother will put the tray of cookies on the table, and the little girl will want to help decorate them with the bowl of icing she’s holding. There’s a good chance the cat will jump up onto the counter to investigate the smell, and someone will have to chase it off. After that, they’ll probably light the candles and sing happy birthday.

t5.intro: You want to upgrade your skills to move into a better job, and you are considering two programs. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Online Project Management Certificate
details: Recorded lectures, no set class times

options.title: Evening Business Diploma (in person)
details: Two years, two evenings a week

other.title: Electrical Apprenticeship
details: Four to five years to complete
You would need to quit your current job

t5.persuade: Your spouse prefers the electrical apprenticeship. Persuade your spouse that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know the apprenticeship sounds appealing because I’d be paid while I learn, and electricians do earn a good living eventually. But I really think the online certificate makes more sense for us right now. First, I’d have to quit my job for the apprenticeship, and twenty dollars an hour is a lot less than I make now. With the mortgage and the kids’ activities, we’d feel that for years. With the certificate, I keep my full salary the whole time. Second, it’s only eight months, not four or five years. I could be applying for project coordinator jobs by next fall. And because it’s self-paced, I can study after the kids are in bed instead of being away two evenings a week. Finally, my back hasn’t been great, so physically demanding work worries me. This is the safer, faster option.

t6.situation: Your fifteen-year-old niece is staying with you for the summer while her parents work abroad. Her parents set a strict 10 p.m. curfew. Your niece has been very responsible, and now she is begging to attend an outdoor concert with two friends that ends at midnight. You trust her, but you promised her parents you would follow their rules.
options: Talk to your niece and explain why she cannot go to the concert.
Talk to your niece’s parents and ask them to let her go.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hi, Marta, thanks for picking up. I know it’s late there, so I’ll be quick. Everything’s fine, but I wanted to ask you something about Sofie. There’s an outdoor concert on Saturday, and she’s asked to go with Lily and Priyanka. The problem is that it ends at midnight, two hours after her curfew. I wouldn’t normally ask, but honestly, she’s been amazing all summer. She’s home on time every night, she helps with dinner, and she even babysat the neighbours’ kids. Here’s what I’m proposing. I’d drive the three girls there, and I’d pick them up at the gate at midnight and bring them straight home. She’d keep her phone on and text me at ten. If you’re not comfortable, I completely understand, and I’ll tell her no myself. But I think she’s earned a little trust.

t7.prompt: Answer the following question: Should parents pay children for doing household chores? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: Personally, I don’t think parents should pay children for basic household chores, although I do think there’s a place for earning money at home. My main reason is that ordinary chores, like making your bed, clearing the table or keeping your room tidy, are part of being a member of a family. Nobody pays the parents for cooking dinner or doing the laundry. If children are paid for everything, they may start to think that helping is optional, or that it only matters when there’s a reward. I’ve actually seen this with my neighbour’s son, who now asks, “How much will you give me?” whenever his mother asks him to carry the groceries. On the other hand, I understand why parents want children to learn about money, and that’s really important. So my solution would be to separate the two. Basic chores are expected and unpaid, but children could earn money for extra jobs that go beyond normal responsibilities, like washing the car, shovelling the driveway or helping with a big garden project. That way, they still learn that work leads to income, and they can practise saving and budgeting. But they also learn that taking care of the home is something everyone does simply because they live there.

scene.alt: A sunny park with a path, where a baby stroller is so enormous that it is as tall as the nearby trees, about the size of a small truck. A man in an orange shirt is pushing it with both hands, and he looks tiny next to it. Three small children walk beside it, and one is waving. A woman on a bench is staring at the giant stroller in surprise, and a dog nearby is looking up at it. There is a pond with a duck, two trees, the sun and a cloud.

t8.prompt: Your friend runs a home daycare and is looking for a way to take several young children on outings. You saw this unusual stroller in a park. Call your friend, describe it, and explain whether you think she should get one. Your friend cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hey, you have to hear what I saw in the park today. A dad was pushing a stroller, but it was gigantic, honestly about the size of a small truck. It was as tall as the trees beside the path, with a huge canopy on top and wheels bigger than a person. The poor guy pushing it looked tiny, like he was pushing a house. Three little kids were walking beside it, and one was waving at everybody. A woman on a bench was staring with her mouth open, and even a dog stopped to look. Now, I know you’ve been looking for a way to take all your daycare kids out at once, but I really don’t think this is it. It wouldn’t fit through a door or on the bus, and imagine pushing it uphill. Maybe a six-seat wagon instead?
